Neonatal Red kangaroos (Macropus rufus) emerge after a remarkably short gestation period of 33 days [tg = 33 days] when maintained at the typical maternal body temperature of 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C]. At birth, the altricial joey weighs a mere 0.817 grams [Wwb = 0.817 grams] and possesses a head length of only 0.89 centimeters [Lb = 0.89 centimeters]. This tiny neonate, which is approximately the size of a jellybean, must immediately embark on a blind crawl from the birth canal to the pouch, where it will permanently attach to a teat for an extended period of lactation. The extreme altriciality of the newborn is a characteristic shared with other macropodids, reflecting an evolutionary strategy that minimizes the energetic burden of gestation on the female. The marsupial birth event itself, while brief, represents a considerable physiological feat given the stark contrast between the neonate’s minute dimensions and the adult female’s massive body size. The subsequent period of pouch life is critical for organogenesis and rapid somatic growth.

The suckling juvenile remains confined to the pouch for a substantial duration, achieving nutritional independence at a definitive developmental milestone. The time since birth at weaning is approximately 235 days since birth [tx = approximately 235 days since birth], a value that aligns closely with field observations of 2 at a temperature of 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C]30 to 250 days. At this point of weaning, the young animal attains a wet weight of 4500 grams [Wwx = 4500 grams] and a head length of 13.3 centimeters . The weaning process is gradual; the joey begins to intermittently leave the pouch and sample vegetation while continuing to suckle, a transitional phase that allows for the gradual maturation of the foregut and the establishment of a cellulolytic microbial community essential for digesting fibrous plant matter. The end of lactation marks a critical transition to full nutritional independence, after which the young red kangaroo must rely entirely on its own foraging efficiency to meet the energetic demands of continued growth and survival in a semi-arid landscape.

Following weaning, the growing juvenile undergoes a prolonged phase of somatic development before attaining sexual maturation. Data from captive populations, maintained at a core temperature of 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C], indicate that the time since birth at puberty averages 483 days after birth [tp = 483 days after birth], although this figure exhibits considerable sexual dimorphism, with females maturing at approximately 517 days and males taking longer at around 806 days. Concurrent with this developmental timeline, the head length at puberty is measured at 16.5 centimeters [Lp = 16.5 centimeters], while the corresponding wet weight at puberty reaches 14,000 grams [Wwp = 14,000 grams]. The onset of puberty is hormonally triggered by a combination of body size, fat reserves, and photoperiodic cues. This species exhibits delayed maturity relative to smaller macropodids, a life-history trait that is consistent with its larger adult body size and the high energetic costs associated with reaching a competitive body mass in a landscape where drought can severely limit food availability.

Adult female Red kangaroos are capable of maintaining a remarkably high reproductive output for a large mammal. Under optimal conditions and at a stable core body temperature of 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C], the maximum reproductive rate is effectively achieved through a strategy where females produce 3 young per litter [N_R_i = 3 young per litter], and typically a single litter every 2.5 years [F_R_i = single litter every 2.5 years]. This is achieved through a sophisticated reproductive strategy known as embryonic diapause, whereby a female can mate and produce a zygote shortly after giving birth, but the development of that new embryo is suspended until the existing joey permanently leaves the pouch or is lost. This mechanism allows for the rapid replacement of offspring and maximizes lifetime fecundity in an unpredictable environment. The average yearly milk production required to support this continuous reproductive cycle has been calculated at approximately 239,342.47 joules per day  at 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C], a substantial energy investment that places a high metabolic demand on the lactating female, who must simultaneously maintain her own body condition while foraging.

The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult Red kangaroo is estimated at 35,000 grams [Wwi = 35,000 grams], a figure derived from mass-length relationships established by Murphy and Smith in 1970 and corroborated by comparative data on grey kangaroos that places Macropus rufus as the largest extant marsupial. This adult body mass is accompanied by a maximum head length of 20.0 centimeters [Li = 20.0 centimeters]. At a stable core temperature of 36.3 °C [T = 36.3 °C], the maximum lifespan documented for this species in a protected setting is 27 years [am = 27 years], a longevity that is considerable for a large mammal and reflects a life-history strategy of delayed maturity, iteroparity, and moderate adult mortality. This long lifespan allows individuals multiple breeding opportunities across variable climatic cycles. The large ultimate body size of Macropus rufus necessitates a highly efficient locomotor system; the species is renowned for its bipedal hopping gait, which minimizes energy expenditure at high speeds. Its physiological adaptations to aridity, including highly efficient kidneys and the ability to select the most nutritious forage, further contribute to its success across the vast interior of the Australian continent.
